title: First ADR for a Payments System
description: Document one payments architecture decision with context and consequences so future teams understand it.
overview: Document one payments architecture decision with context and consequences so future teams understand it.
tasks: Pick one real decision, such as the database choice, the queue, or the deployment platform.
Create docs/adr/0001-title.md using the sections Title, Status, Context, Decision, Options considered, and Consequences.
List at least three options and one reason each was chosen or rejected.
State at least two consequences, one good and one bad, and who must act on them.
Link the ADR from the README and add a second ADR that supersedes it to practise status changes.

examples.title: Sample ADR
examples.code:
# 0001. Use PostgreSQL for orders
Status: Accepted
Context: We need transactions and reporting queries.
Decision: Use PostgreSQL 16.
Options: PostgreSQL, MongoDB, DynamoDB
Consequences: Strong consistency, but we must manage backups ourselves.
examples.output: Anyone can read the file in two minutes and understand why PostgreSQL was chosen and what it costs.

notes: Write the context before the decision. A reader should agree with the problem before they see the answer.
Never edit an accepted ADR. Write a new one that supersedes it.

title: C4 Diagrams for a Payments System
description: Describe a payments system at context and container levels so everyone understands how payments flow.
overview: Describe a payments system at context and container levels so everyone understands how payments flow.
tasks: Pick a system with at least four parts, such as a web app, an API, a database, and an external service.
Draw the context diagram: your system in the centre, the users, and each external system, with labelled arrows.
Draw the container diagram: each deployable unit, its technology, and how containers talk to each other.
Label every arrow with a verb and a protocol, for example 'reads orders over HTTPS'.
Ask someone who does not know the system to explain it back to you using only the diagrams.

examples.title: Sample container list
examples.code:
Web app (React) -> API (Node.js): calls over HTTPS/JSON
API (Node.js) -> Database (PostgreSQL): reads and writes over TCP
API (Node.js) -> Payment provider: sends charges over HTTPS
examples.output: Every container has a name, a technology, and at least one labelled relationship.

notes: Use a tool such as Structurizr, draw.io, or Mermaid. The tool matters less than the labels.
Do not mix levels. Containers go in the container diagram, not the context diagram.

title: Trade-offs for a Payments Platform
description: Compare two payments architectures against quality attributes so customers get reliable payments.
overview: Compare two payments architectures against quality attributes so customers get reliable payments.
tasks: Choose a system and two candidate architectures, for example monolith versus microservices.
Build a utility tree with at least five quality attributes such as performance, availability, security, modifiability, and cost.
Write each as a measurable scenario, for example '95 percent of checkouts complete in under 2 seconds at 500 requests per second'.
Score each architecture against each scenario from 1 to 5 and explain every score in one sentence.
Identify at least two risks and one trade-off point where improving one attribute hurts another.
Write a one-page recommendation.

examples.title: Sample scoring table
examples.code:
Scenario                          Monolith  Microservices
Checkout under 2s at 500 rps      4         3
Deploy one change in under 1 hour 2         5
Run cost under $2000 per month    5         2
examples.output: Totals: Monolith 11, Microservices 10. The result depends on weights, so state your weights and justify them.

notes: A scenario without a number cannot be tested. Rewrite it until it has one.
Show the analysis to the people who will own the system before you finalise.

title: Migrate a Banking Monolith to Services
description: Plan an incremental migration of a banking monolith so customer services never go down.
overview: Plan an incremental migration of a banking monolith so customer services never go down.
tasks: Describe the current monolith and list its modules with their dependencies.
Choose one module to extract first and justify it using change frequency, coupling, and team ownership.
Define the new service's API and the data it owns, and explain how data will be split safely.
Describe how traffic moves gradually: a routing layer, a feature flag, and a percentage rollout.
Write the rollback plan and the metrics that trigger it.
List what you will not extract yet and why.

examples.title: Sample rollout plan
examples.code:
Week 1: 1 percent of read traffic to the new service
Week 2: 10 percent, compare error rate and latency
Week 3: 50 percent
Week 4: 100 percent, keep the old code for 2 weeks
examples.output: Each step has a metric and a rollback trigger, for example 'roll back if p95 latency is 20 percent worse'.

notes: The hardest part is data. Do not share one database between two services for long.
If you cannot name the benefit of splitting, do not split.

title: Fitness Functions for Banking Architecture
description: Turn banking architecture goals into automated checks so customer data rules are enforced.
overview: Turn banking architecture goals into automated checks so customer data rules are enforced.
tasks: List five architectural rules for a codebase, for example 'the domain layer must not import the web layer'.
Implement at least three as automated checks using a tool such as ArchUnit, dependency-cruiser, or a custom script.
Add a performance or size budget check, for example 'bundle size under 300 KB'.
Run the checks in CI and make the build fail on a violation.
Deliberately break each rule once to prove the check catches it.

examples.title: Sample check output
examples.code:
FAIL  src/domain/order.js imports src/web/controller.js
rule: domain must not depend on web
examples.output: The build fails and names the file and the rule that was broken.

notes: A rule nobody enforces is a wish. If it matters, automate it.
Keep the number of rules small so people trust them.

title: Well-Architected Review of a Payments System
description: Review a payments system for reliability and security so customers can rely on it.
overview: Review a payments system for reliability and security so customers can rely on it.
tasks: Pick a system and describe it in one page with a diagram.
Review it against six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance, cost, and sustainability.
Write at least three findings per pillar with evidence, a risk level, and a recommended fix.
Prioritise findings by risk and effort, and choose the top five.
Estimate the cost and time of the top five fixes.
Present the review in 20 minutes and record the decisions.

examples.title: Sample finding
examples.code:
Pillar: Reliability
Finding: single database instance, no tested restore
Risk: High
Fix: add a replica and run a quarterly restore drill
Effort: 3 days
examples.output: Each finding names evidence, risk, a fix, and effort so leadership can decide.

notes: Findings need evidence such as metrics, configs, or incident history, not opinions.
End with decisions and owners, not just a report.

title: Event-Driven Payments Architecture
description: Design an event-driven payments system with failure handling so no payment is silently lost.
overview: Design an event-driven payments system with failure handling so no payment is silently lost.
tasks: Define at least eight domain events with names in the past tense and a schema for each.
Draw the flow of events between services with sequence diagrams for the happy path and one failure path.
Decide delivery guarantees, ordering rules, and idempotency for each consumer.
Design the dead-letter queue, retry policy, and replay procedure.
Describe schema evolution rules so producers can change without breaking consumers.
Write the observability plan: tracing across events and alerts on lag.

examples.title: Sample event
examples.code: {"type":"OrderPlaced","version":1,"orderId":"o-123","total":42.5,"occurredAt":"2026-02-01T10:00:00Z"}
examples.output: Consumers must handle the same event twice without a duplicate effect, so every handler is idempotent.

notes: Events describe facts that happened, not commands.
Decide who owns each schema before the first producer ships.

title: Tech Radar for a Fintech Organisation
description: Create a tech radar and governance process so a fintech chooses safe, supported tools.
overview: Create a tech radar and governance process so a fintech chooses safe, supported tools.
tasks: Inventory the technologies used across your teams and classify each as adopt, trial, assess, or hold.
Publish the radar as a page with a short rationale for each entry.
Define an architecture review process: when a review is needed, who attends, and how decisions are recorded as ADRs.
Define criteria for adding a new technology, such as support cost, hiring, security, and fit.
Run one review for a real proposal and record the outcome.
Set a quarterly cadence to update the radar.

examples.title: Sample radar rows
examples.code:
Adopt   PostgreSQL     primary relational database
Trial   Kafka          event streaming, one team
Hold    Self-hosted Mongo   migrate to managed service
examples.output: Teams can see at a glance what to use, what to try, and what to stop using.

notes: Governance should speed teams up. If reviews take weeks, simplify them.
Make decisions public so people learn from them.

title: Disaster Recovery Design for Banking
description: Design and rehearse recovery from a regional outage so customers keep access to their money.
overview: Design and rehearse recovery from a regional outage so customers keep access to their money.
tasks: Define the recovery time objective and recovery point objective for each component.
Choose a strategy per component: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, or active-active, and justify the cost.
Design data replication, DNS or traffic failover, and secrets and configuration replication.
Write the runbook with exact steps and owners.
Run a game day: simulate the region failure and measure real recovery time.
Write a report with gaps found and fixes planned.

examples.title: Sample objectives
examples.code:
Checkout API: RTO 15 min, RPO 1 min  -> warm standby
Reports:      RTO 4 hours, RPO 24 hours -> backup and restore
examples.output: Different components get different strategies, because the cost of active-active is high.

notes: An untested recovery plan is a guess.
Include people and communication in the plan, not only systems.

title: Team Charter for a Payments Squad
description: Write a charter and working agreements so a payments squad works together for customers.
overview: Write a charter and working agreements so a payments squad works together for customers.
tasks: Write the team's mission and the systems and services it owns in one page.
List who the team depends on and who depends on it.
Run a 45-minute workshop and agree on five working agreements, for example response times and code review expectations.
Define how the team makes decisions and handles disagreements.
Publish the charter and schedule a review in three months.

examples.title: Sample working agreements
examples.code:
1. Pull requests get a first review within 1 working day.
2. We write down decisions in ADRs.
3. No meetings on Wednesday mornings.
examples.output: Each agreement is specific enough that anyone can tell whether it is being followed.

notes: Agreements the team writes itself are followed far more than rules handed down.
Keep it to one page.

title: Interview Scorecard for a Fintech Engineer
description: Create a structured interview scorecard so fintechs hire engineers fairly.
overview: Create a structured interview scorecard so fintechs hire engineers fairly.
tasks: Define the role's five most important competencies.
Write two questions per competency and a description of weak, good, and strong answers.
Create a 1 to 4 rating scale with written anchors and a place for evidence notes.
Define a debrief process where interviewers submit scores before discussing.
Run a mock interview with a colleague and refine the scorecard.

examples.title: Sample scorecard row
examples.code:
Competency: debugging
Question: Walk me through the hardest bug you fixed.
Strong: forms hypotheses, narrows systematically, prevents recurrence
Score: 3
Evidence: used logs to isolate the service, added a regression test
examples.output: Every score is backed by written evidence that others can review.

notes: Ask every candidate for the same role the same core questions.
Submit scores before the debrief to reduce groupthink.

title: Career Ladder for Fintech Engineers
description: Define levels and expectations for fintech engineers so growth is clear and fair.
overview: Define levels and expectations for fintech engineers so growth is clear and fair.
tasks: Define four to five levels, for example junior to staff.
Choose four dimensions such as technical skill, delivery, collaboration, and impact.
Write observable behaviours for each dimension at each level.
Write a promotion process with who decides, what evidence is needed, and how often.
Test the ladder by placing three real engineers on it and checking whether they agree.
Collect feedback from the team and revise.

examples.title: Sample ladder row
examples.code:
Dimension: Impact
Mid:    delivers well-scoped features without guidance
Senior: leads a project across two teams and unblocks others
Staff:  sets technical direction that affects the whole organisation
examples.output: Each cell describes behaviours that a manager can point to in someone's work.

notes: Describe behaviours, not years of experience.
Revisit the ladder every year.

title: DORA Metrics for a Payments Team
description: Measure delivery speed and stability so payment fixes reach customers faster.
overview: Measure delivery speed and stability so payment fixes reach customers faster.
tasks: Define deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore service for your team.
Collect the data from your repository, CI, and incident tracker with a script.
Build a simple dashboard or weekly report showing a 12-week trend.
Pick the weakest metric and propose two improvements.
Agree with the team that the metrics are for learning and never for ranking individuals.

examples.title: Sample weekly row
examples.code: Week 12: deploys 14, lead time 1.8 days, change failure 7 percent, restore time 42 minutes
examples.output: The trend shows whether changes improve delivery, and the weakest metric guides the next experiment.

notes: Never use these numbers to compare individuals.
Look at trends over weeks, not one data point.

title: On-Call Rotation for Payment Operations
description: Design a fair on-call rotation so payments are restored quickly when they fail.
overview: Design a fair on-call rotation so payments are restored quickly when they fail.
tasks: Define the rotation length, handover time, and a fair compensation or time-off policy.
Define severity levels with examples and expected response times.
Write the incident roles: incident commander, communications lead, and responders.
Write a runbook template and create runbooks for the three most common alerts.
Run a practice incident and review it in a blameless session.
Track alert volume and set a goal to reduce noisy alerts.

examples.title: Sample severity table
examples.code:
SEV1: customers cannot check out   respond in 5 minutes, page the incident commander
SEV2: degraded performance        respond in 30 minutes
SEV3: internal tool issue         next business day
examples.output: Anyone can classify an alert and know who to wake up and how fast.

notes: Measure pages per week per person. If it is high, fix alerts before adding people.
Always follow an incident with actions and owners.

title: Quarterly Capacity Plan for a Fintech Team
description: Plan a quarter with realistic capacity so customer-facing fixes ship on time.
overview: Plan a quarter with realistic capacity so customer-facing fixes ship on time.
tasks: Calculate team capacity in engineer-weeks after holidays, leave, on-call, and meetings.
List candidate work items with a size estimate and business value.
Reserve capacity for unplanned work, bugs, and tech debt, for example 20 percent.
Pick the work that fits, and write down what you are deliberately not doing.
Share the plan with stakeholders and agree on how changes will be handled.
Review at the end of the quarter: planned versus delivered.

examples.title: Sample capacity calculation
examples.code:
6 engineers x 13 weeks = 78 engineer-weeks
minus leave and holidays 8, on-call 6, meetings and support 10
Available: 54. Reserve 20 percent (11) for unplanned work. Plan: 43 engineer-weeks
examples.output: The team commits to 43 engineer-weeks of planned work, not 78.

notes: Overcommitting hurts trust more than saying no.
Show the 'not doing' list to stakeholders.

title: Review Calibration for Banking Engineers
description: Design a fair review and calibration process so banking engineers are judged consistently.
overview: Design a fair review and calibration process so banking engineers are judged consistently.
tasks: Define the rating scale with written descriptions tied to your career ladder.
Create the self-review, peer feedback, and manager review templates.
Define the timeline from feedback collection to results.
Run a calibration meeting format: how managers present evidence and how differences are resolved.
Add bias checks such as comparing rating distributions by team, tenure, and gender.
Write a guide for delivering difficult feedback and a growth plan template.

examples.title: Sample bias check
examples.code:
Team A rated 'exceeds' 40 percent, Team B 10 percent
Action: managers re-present evidence for Team A; adjust where evidence is weak
examples.output: Differences are investigated with evidence rather than accepted as they are.

notes: Ratings are only as fair as the evidence collected during the year, so collect it continuously.
No surprises: nobody should hear a serious issue for the first time in a review.

title: Tech Debt Business Case for Payments
description: Make the business case for paying down payments tech debt so customer outages decline.
overview: Make the business case for paying down payments tech debt so customer outages decline.
tasks: Inventory the top ten pieces of debt with owner, area, and description.
Estimate the cost of each: incidents, slowed delivery, and risk, using data such as time spent and outages.
Prioritise by cost versus effort and pick a plan for the next two quarters.
Propose a funding model such as a fixed percentage of capacity or a dedicated team.
Define how you will show results: lead time, incident count, or build time.
Present to leadership with a clear ask and a measurable outcome.

examples.title: Sample debt entry
examples.code:
Debt: flaky integration tests
Cost: 6 engineer-hours per week lost to reruns, 2 delayed releases last quarter
Fix: 3 engineer-weeks
Payback: about 6 months
examples.output: Leadership sees cost, effort, and payback, so they can compare it with a new feature.

notes: Speak in outcomes such as speed, risk, and cost, not in code quality.
Deliver one visible win early to build trust.

title: Engineering Budget for a Fintech
description: Build a yearly budget and headcount plan so a fintech funds reliable services.
overview: Build a yearly budget and headcount plan so a fintech funds reliable services.
tasks: List all cost categories: salaries, contractors, cloud, tooling, training, and recruiting.
Forecast cloud and tooling costs with growth assumptions.
Build a headcount plan with roles, start dates, and the work each hire unlocks.
Create three scenarios: lean, expected, and growth, with the impact of each on the roadmap.
Define cost-saving options and their risks.
Present the plan and record the approved budget and open questions.

examples.title: Sample scenarios
examples.code:
Lean: 0 hires, roadmap items 1-3 only
Expected: 3 hires in Q2, items 1-6
Growth: 6 hires, items 1-9, adds a platform team
examples.output: Leadership can see what each budget level buys and what it leaves out.

notes: Tie every hire to a specific outcome.
Track actual spend against the plan monthly.

title: Hiring Pipeline for a Fintech Team
description: Design an end-to-end hiring pipeline with metrics so fintechs hire people who serve customers well.
overview: Design an end-to-end hiring pipeline with metrics so fintechs hire people who serve customers well.
tasks: Write a job description focused on outcomes and the real requirements.
Define the stages: screen, technical interview, team interview, and decision, with who runs each and the scorecard used.
Create a candidate experience plan with response-time commitments and feedback.
Define the offer process and compensation bands.
Track funnel metrics: applicants, pass rate per stage, time to hire, and offer acceptance.
Review the funnel after three months and fix the biggest drop-off.

examples.title: Sample funnel
examples.code: Applicants 200 -> screen 40 -> technical 15 -> team 6 -> offers 3 -> accepted 2
examples.output: Pass rates per stage show where candidates are lost and whether the process is too slow.

notes: Speed matters. Strong candidates accept other offers within weeks.
Train every interviewer and use the same scorecard.

title: Payments CLI for Merchants Org-Wide
description: Release a payments command-line tool to 500 engineers on every platform so merchants' reconciliation works everywhere.
overview: Release a payments command-line tool to 500 engineers on every platform so merchants' reconciliation works everywhere.
tasks: Build reproducible release artefacts for darwin-arm64, darwin-amd64, linux-amd64, linux-arm64 and windows-amd64 from one tagged commit using GoReleaser or cargo-dist; two builds of the same tag must produce identical SHA-256 sums
Sign artefacts with cosign keyless signing and notarise the macOS binary; publish a checksums file and an SBOM in SPDX format
Provide install paths through Homebrew tap, a curl install script that verifies checksums, apt/yum repo or winget manifest, and a container image under 20 MB

Implement a self-update command that checks at most once per 24 hours, never blocks startup for more than 50 ms, verifies the signature before swapping the binary, and rolls back on a failed post-update smoke test
Define a compatibility contract: flags, exit codes and --output json schemas are semver-governed; add a golden-file test suite that fails CI on any breaking change to documented output
Add opt-in anonymous telemetry (command name, duration, exit code, version, OS) with a documented schema, a one-line opt-out via env var, and a CI check that no argument values are ever sent
Support deprecation: a flag marked deprecated prints one warning on stderr per day, never on stdout, and is removed only after two minor releases
Run a canary rollout: 5 percent of users for 3 days, with an automatic halt if crash-rate exceeds 0.5 percent of invocations
Deliver a dashboard showing version adoption, p95 startup time and top error codes, and a measured result such as 90 percent of active users on the latest version within 14 days

examples.title: Verify a release before installing
examples.code:
$ cosign verify-blob --certificate-identity-regexp 'github.com/acme/acme-cli' \
    --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
    --signature acme_1.8.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz.sig \
    --certificate acme_1.8.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz.pem \
    acme_1.8.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz
$ sha256sum -c checksums.txt --ignore-missing
examples.output:
Verified OK
acme_1.8.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz: OK

examples.title: Golden-file contract test
examples.code: $ acme deploy list --output json | jq 'keys'
examples.output:
["items","next_cursor","schema_version"]
# CI diffs this against testdata/deploy_list.golden.json; any removed key fails the build

notes: Never write update logic that replaces a running executable in place on Windows; rename the old file first, because a running exe cannot be overwritten.
Stdout is an API. Anything that is not the result (progress, warnings, update notices) goes to stderr, or you will break every script that pipes your tool.
Telemetry without a published schema and an easy opt-out will be removed by your security team; design it with them first.

title: Fast Payments CLI for Reconciliation
description: Make a payments CLI start under 30 ms and print machine-readable output so small shops reconcile daily sales quickly.
overview: Make a payments CLI start under 30 ms and print machine-readable output so small shops reconcile daily sales quickly.
tasks: Measure baseline with hyperfine (50 runs, 5 warmups) for help, version and a typical command; record mean, p95 and peak RSS in a table

Trace startup using strace -c or dtruss and a language profiler (py-spy, node --cpu-prof, or pprof); cut cold start for --version to under 30 ms by lazy-importing heavy modules and removing eager config network calls
Detect TTY with isatty on stdin, stdout and stderr separately; disable colour, spinners and prompts when not a TTY, and honour NO_COLOR and CLICOLOR_FORCE
Add --output json and --output ndjson with stable schemas; streaming commands must flush per record so a downstream head -n 1 returns in under 100 ms
Handle SIGPIPE and SIGINT: exit quietly with status 141 style behaviour on a closed pipe, and clean up temp files and child processes on Ctrl-C within 1 second
Define and document exit codes (0 success, 1 generic failure, 2 usage error, 3 not found, 4 auth failure, 75 temporary failure) and test each in an integration suite
Generate shell completions for bash, zsh and fish, including dynamic completion of remote resource names with a 200 ms timeout and a cache
Add a test matrix that runs the binary under LANG=C, a UTF-8 locale and a 40-column terminal, verifying no mojibake and no wrapping of machine output
Report results: startup reduced by at least 20x, zero failing pipe or CI scenarios, and a before/after table committed to the repo

examples.title: Benchmark before and after
examples.code: $ hyperfine --warmup 5 --runs 50 'acme --version' 'acme-old --version'
examples.output:
Benchmark 1: acme --version
  Time (mean ± σ):      24.1 ms ±   1.8 ms
Benchmark 2: acme-old --version
  Time (mean ± σ):     873.4 ms ±  31.2 ms
# values vary by machine

examples.title: Pipe behaviour test
examples.code: $ acme events stream --output ndjson | head -n 1; echo "${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
examples.output:
{"id":"ev_1","type":"deploy"}
141

notes: Most startup time is import and config loading, not your logic; profile with a flame graph before optimising anything.
Prompts in non-interactive mode must fail with exit code 2 and a message naming the flag that supplies the answer, never hang waiting on stdin.
Do not change exit codes casually; scripts depend on them as much as on output.

title: CLI Plugin Architecture for Banking Tools
description: Build an extension system so other teams add banking subcommands safely, with versioned contracts.
overview: Build an extension system so other teams add banking subcommands safely, with versioned contracts.
tasks: Write a design document comparing three models (executables named acme-foo on PATH like git and kubectl, in-process dynamic loading, and a JSON-RPC subprocess protocol); pick one and record rejected options in an ADR
Implement discovery: scan a configured plugin directory and PATH, resolve name collisions deterministically, and refuse plugins that shadow core commands

Specify a versioned protocol: plugins receive context (config, auth token handle, output format, terminal width) through environment variables or stdin JSON with a protocol_version field, and the host rejects incompatible versions with a clear message
Provide an SDK in two languages that handles flag parsing, help registration, structured output and error codes, so a minimal plugin is under 30 lines
Never pass raw credentials to plugins; issue short-lived scoped tokens with 5 minute expiry, and log which plugin requested which scope
Add acme plugin install, list, verify and remove, with plugins distributed as signed archives and pinned by digest in a lockfile
Include a conformance test kit that plugin authors run in CI; the host runs it against the 10 most-used plugins on every core release
Measure and cap overhead: plugin discovery adds under 10 ms to startup using a cached index invalidated by directory mtime
Migrate three existing in-tree commands to plugins without changing user-visible behaviour, proven by golden tests

examples.title: Host to plugin handshake
examples.code:
{"protocol_version": 2,
 "command": ["report", "cost"],
 "output": "json",
 "term_width": 120,
 "auth": {"token_env": "ACME_PLUGIN_TOKEN", "scopes": ["billing:read"], "expires_in": 300}}
examples.output: Plugin writes a JSON result to stdout and exits 0; protocol mismatch makes the host exit 3 with: plugin acme-report requires protocol 3, host supports 2

examples.title: Minimal plugin
examples.output:
$ acme report cost --team data
TEAM  USD
data  1240.50

notes: The protocol is your public API; add fields freely but never repurpose or remove one without a major version.
Plugins that crash must not take down the host or corrupt its terminal state; always restore the TTY in a finally path.
Trust is the hard part: unsigned plugins from arbitrary URLs are remote code execution with your users' credentials.

title: Zero-Downtime Move of a Payments Web App
description: Move a live payments web app and its database to a new platform with no downtime, so customers can always pay.
overview: Move a live payments web app and its database to a new platform with no downtime, so customers can always pay.
tasks: Write a migration plan with a dependency inventory, a risk register and explicit go/no-go criteria such as error rate under 0.1 percent and p95 latency within 10 percent of baseline

Replicate the database with logical replication (pg_logical or native publication) to the new cluster, and verify with row counts plus checksums on 20 sampled tables; replication lag must stay under 5 seconds before cutover
Apply expand/contract migrations: every schema change is backward compatible with the previous app version so old and new versions run at the same time
Put both stacks behind a weighted load balancer or DNS with 60 second TTL; shift traffic 1, 5, 25, 50, 100 percent with a soak of 30 minutes at each step and automatic rollback on SLO breach
Handle sessions and caches: move sessions to a shared store before the first shift so users are not logged out, and warm caches on the new stack
Rehearse the full cutover twice on a production-sized copy, timing each step and recording the measured write freeze, which must be under 10 seconds
Prepare and test rollback: reverse replication from new to old so reverting after cutover loses zero writes
Run a synthetic user journey every 30 seconds on both stacks throughout and publish the availability graph
After cutover keep the old stack read-only for 14 days, then decommission, and publish a retrospective with cost, latency and incident numbers

examples.title: Replication lag check
examples.code:
SELECT application_name, state,
       pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn) AS lag_bytes,
       replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;
examples.output:
application_name | state     | lag_bytes | replay_lag
 new_cluster_sub  | streaming |      4096 | 00:00:00.8
(1 row)   -- values vary

examples.title: Cutover runbook excerpt
examples.code:
T-30m  freeze deploys, announce in #ops
T-5m   confirm lag < 5s, error budget > 50%
T-0    set old DB read-only; wait lag = 0; promote new; flip pool
T+2m   verify checks A1-A6; if any fail, run rollback step R1
examples.output: Each step has an owner, a command, an expected output and a time limit; the runbook is rehearsed, not improvised.

notes: Sequences, large objects and extensions are not copied by logical replication; list them in the plan or you will find out at cutover.
DNS TTLs are advisory; some clients cache for hours, so keep the old endpoint serving correctly until traffic is verified at zero.
The rollback you have not rehearsed does not exist.

title: Banking Web App Performance Budget
description: Bring a large banking web app's p75 load time under 2.5 s, so customers on slow connections can check balances.
overview: Bring a large banking web app's p75 load time under 2.5 s, so customers on slow connections can check balances.
tasks: Instrument real-user monitoring with the web-vitals library sending LCP, INP, CLS and TTFB with route, device class and connection type to your analytics store; collect at least one week of data
Segment p75 and p95 by route and device and rank the top 5 routes by user-weighted pain, not by raw score

Set a performance budget in CI (for example JS under 170 KB gzipped per route, LCP under 2.5 s on a throttled Moto G class profile) using Lighthouse CI or WebPageTest and fail pull requests that exceed it
Analyse the bundle with source-map-explorer or webpack-bundle-analyzer, then apply route-level code splitting, dependency replacement and tree-shaking to remove at least 40 percent of initial JS
Fix server side: enable Brotli, HTTP caching with immutable fingerprinted assets, a CDN, preconnect and early hints, and streaming SSR so TTFB p75 is under 600 ms
Diagnose INP with the Chrome performance panel and long animation frames; break up tasks over 50 ms with scheduler.yield or web workers
Eliminate layout shift with explicit image dimensions, font-display and reserved ad or embed slots, bringing CLS p75 under 0.1
Run an A/B experiment or a staged rollout and correlate the improvement to a business metric such as conversion or bounce rate
Document the findings and the budget policy in a playbook other teams can follow

examples.title: Field data collection
examples.output: POST /rum {"name":"LCP","value":4812,"route":"/checkout","target":"img.hero"}  -- one beacon per metric per page view

examples.title: Before and after summary
examples.code:
Route /checkout  (p75, mobile, 28 days)
               before   after
LCP            4.8 s    2.3 s
INP            380 ms   150 ms
Initial JS     1.9 MB   0.9 MB (gzip 310 KB -> 148 KB)
examples.output: Shape of the deliverable; actual numbers vary

notes: Lab scores guide debugging but field data decides success; Google evaluates the 75th percentile of real users.
Third-party scripts are often the largest cost and the hardest politics; quantify their INP and LCP impact and make owners accountable.
A budget enforced only in a dashboard drifts; enforce it in CI.

title: Payments Web App Security Hardening
description: Threat-model a payments web app and close critical findings so customers' logins and cards stay safe.
overview: Threat-model a payments web app and close critical findings so customers' logins and cards stay safe.
tasks: Produce a STRIDE threat model with data-flow diagrams for login, file upload, billing and admin; rank at least 15 threats and map each to a control or accepted risk

Harden sessions: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax cookies, rotation on login and privilege change, idle timeout 30 minutes, absolute timeout 12 hours, and step-up authentication for sensitive actions; add TOTP or WebAuthn
Deploy a strict Content-Security-Policy with nonces, plus HSTS with preload, frame-ancestors, Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy; start in report-only for 2 weeks and drive violations to zero

Enforce tenant isolation in depth: every query scoped by tenant id through a single data-access layer or PostgreSQL row-level security, with an automated test that tries cross-tenant access on every endpoint and expects 404
Add dependency and supply-chain controls: lockfiles, SCA scanning with a 7 day SLA for criticals, pinned CI actions by commit SHA, and signed container images
Run SAST, DAST (OWASP ZAP in CI) and a manual test of the OWASP Top 10 and ASVS level 2 checklist; track findings in a register with severity, owner and due date
Remediate all critical and high findings from the external pen test within 30 days and re-test; show zero open criticals
Add detection: structured audit logs for auth events, alerts on credential-stuffing patterns (more than 20 failed logins per IP per minute) and a tested incident response runbook
Present an evidence pack mapping controls to SOC 2 criteria

examples.title: Cross-tenant authorisation test
examples.output: === 112 passed in 9.4s ===   (route count varies; a single failure blocks the build)

examples.title: CSP header
examples.code: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-r4nd0m'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'; report-to csp
examples.output: Browser blocks inline scripts without the nonce and posts violation reports to the collector

notes: IDOR and broken tenant isolation are the highest-impact bugs in SaaS; test them systematically rather than hoping reviews catch them.
Rolling out CSP in enforce mode on day one breaks third-party widgets; use report-only and fix by data.
A finding is closed only when the pen-tester re-tests it, not when the ticket is marked done.

title: Payments API Platform Standards
description: Create an organisation-wide API standard with versioning and deprecation so payment integrations don't break for merchants.
overview: Create an organisation-wide API standard with versioning and deprecation so payment integrations don't break for merchants.
tasks: Write an API style guide covering resource naming, HTTP semantics, idempotency keys, cursor pagination, filtering, error format (RFC 9457 problem details), rate-limit headers and ISO 8601 timestamps
Encode at least 25 rules as Spectral rulesets run in CI against every OpenAPI 3.1 spec, with severity levels and an exemptions file requiring a linked justification

Define versioning and deprecation policy: additive changes need no version, breaking changes need a new major, deprecated endpoints emit Deprecation and Sunset headers and are supported at least 12 months
Add breaking-change detection with oasdiff on every pull request, blocking merges that remove fields, narrow types or add required request fields
Set up an API review board process with a design-first template and a 3 business day SLA; measure review lead time
Publish a developer portal with generated reference docs, runnable examples, SDKs generated in 3 languages, and a changelog
Build consumer-driven contract tests with Pact for the 5 most depended-on services, run in provider CI

Report adoption metrics: percentage of endpoints passing lint (target 95 percent in 2 quarters), mean time to first successful call for a new partner (target under 30 minutes), and number of breaking changes shipped without notice (target zero)

examples.title: Spectral rule
examples.code:
rules:
  list-must-paginate:
    description: Collection GET responses must define next_cursor
    given: "$.paths[*].get.responses.200.content.application/json.schema"
    severity: error
    then:
      field: properties.next_cursor
      function: truthy
examples.output:
/specs/orders.yaml
  42:9  error  list-must-paginate  Collection GET responses must define next_cursor
 x 1 problem (1 error)

examples.title: Deprecation headers
examples.code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Deprecation: @1767225600
Sunset: Wed, 31 Dec 2026 23:59:59 GMT
Link: <https://api.acme.com/docs/migrate-v2>; rel="deprecation"
examples.output: Clients and monitoring can detect usage of a deprecated endpoint programmatically

notes: A standard nobody can run automatically is a wiki page; every rule should be a linter check or a test.
Grandfather old services with a dated exemption and a migration owner rather than demanding a big-bang fix.
Measure who still calls deprecated endpoints, per API key, before announcing a sunset date.

title: Payments API Reliability Under Load
description: Define SLOs and rate limits so a payments API holds 5,000 requests per second during shopping peaks.
overview: Define SLOs and rate limits so a payments API holds 5,000 requests per second during shopping peaks.
tasks: Define SLIs and SLOs: availability 99.95 percent over 30 days, p99 latency under 400 ms for reads, with error budget policy that freezes feature launches when 100 percent of the budget is burned

Implement per-tenant rate limiting with a token bucket in Redis (atomic Lua script), returning 429 with Retry-After and RateLimit headers; test fairness so one tenant at 10x quota cannot raise another tenant's p99 by more than 10 percent
Add load shedding: a concurrency limiter plus priority queues that reject low-priority traffic with 503 when queue delay exceeds 100 ms, keeping health checks and writes alive
Enforce deadlines and cascading timeouts so downstream timeout is always shorter than upstream; cap retries to 2 with exponential backoff, jitter and a retry budget of 10 percent of traffic
Make writes safe to retry with Idempotency-Key storage for 24 hours and a test that replays a POST 50 times and creates one record
Write k6 or Gatling scenarios for steady load (5,000 rps for 30 minutes), spike (0 to 8,000 rps in 10 seconds), soak (6 hours) and dependency failure; run in a production-like environment
Inject faults (add 500 ms latency to the database, kill 1 of 3 instances) and verify SLOs hold or degrade as designed
Build burn-rate alerts (14.4x over 1 hour and 6x over 6 hours) and a dashboard, and write a capacity model stating the headroom per instance
Publish results: breaking point, bottleneck found, and fixes made

examples.title: k6 scenario
examples.output:
✓ http_req_failed.. rate=0.02%
✓ http_req_duration p(99)=312ms   (values vary with environment)

examples.title: Rate limit response
examples.code:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 2
RateLimit-Limit: 1000
RateLimit-Remaining: 0
Content-Type: application/problem+json
examples.output: Client backs off for 2 seconds; the body names the limit that was exceeded

notes: Use open-model (arrival rate) load tests; closed-model virtual users slow down when the server slows and hide overload.
Retries multiply load exactly when the system is weakest; a retry budget is as important as the limit itself.
Averages hide everything; alert on burn rate of percentile-based SLIs.

title: Payments API Version Migration
description: Retire an old payments API used by 300 clients with a compatibility layer, so merchants keep accepting payments.
overview: Retire an old payments API used by 300 clients with a compatibility layer, so merchants keep accepting payments.
tasks: Instrument every request with API key, client version and endpoint, and build a usage report ranking consumers by traffic and by revenue; identify the 20 clients that make up 90 percent of calls

Implement v1 as an adapter over the v2 core (translation layer in the gateway) so there is one business logic path; prove equivalence by shadow-comparing responses on 1 percent of v1 traffic and logging diffs
Write a migration guide with a field-by-field mapping table, code diffs and a codemod or SDK upgrade for the two most common client languages
Create a sandbox with replayed sample data and a v1-to-v2 compatibility checker that consumers can run against their own recorded traffic

Publish a timeline: announce, deprecation headers at month 0, brownouts of 1 hour then 4 hours then 24 hours at months 6, 8 and 10, sunset at month 12; communicate through email, portal banners and account managers
Run scheduled brownouts returning 410 Gone with a link to the guide, and track which consumers react
Provide a per-consumer migration dashboard for account managers and escalate any consumer above 1 percent of traffic that has not started 90 days before sunset
Complete the shutdown with a final read-only grace period and a kill switch ready to re-enable for 14 days; measure the end state, such as zero v1 calls and fewer than 5 support tickets per week

examples.title: Usage query
examples.code:
SELECT api_key, count(*) AS calls, max(ts) AS last_seen
FROM api_requests
WHERE version = 'v1' AND ts > now() - interval '30 days'
GROUP BY api_key ORDER BY calls DESC LIMIT 5;

examples.title: Shadow diff log line
examples.code: {"endpoint":"GET /v1/orders/881","diff":[{"path":"$.total","v1":"12.50","v2_adapted":12.5}],"severity":"type_change"}
examples.output: Diffs are grouped by path; the goal is zero unexplained diffs before the adapter serves real traffic

notes: Mobile clients linger for years; look at version distribution before choosing a sunset date, and plan for a forced-update screen.
Brownouts find forgotten integrations cheaply; a surprise outage on sunset day is the expensive way.
Keep a rollback switch after shutdown; someone always has a quarterly batch job.

title: Crawler for Public Financial Pages
description: Design a polite crawler that fetches 50 million public financial pages so consumers can compare offers.
overview: Design a polite crawler that fetches 50 million public financial pages so consumers can compare offers.
tasks: Design the URL frontier with per-host queues, a priority function combining freshness decay, importance and depth, and a min-heap of next-allowed-fetch times per host so no host exceeds its limit

Honour robots.txt (cache 24 hours, respect Crawl-delay and Disallow), send an identifying User-Agent with a contact URL, and enforce a default 1 request per second per host with adaptive back-off on 429 and 5xx

Run stateless fetcher workers on a queue (Kafka or Redis streams) with at-least-once delivery and idempotent writes keyed by a URL fingerprint plus content hash, giving effectively exactly-once storage

Deduplicate URLs with canonicalisation (lowercase host, strip tracking params, sort query keys) and a Bloom filter sized for 500 million URLs at 0.1 percent false positive rate; deduplicate near-identical content with SimHash
Detect change efficiently using ETag, If-Modified-Since and content hashes, and adapt revisit interval per page from observed change rate
Store raw responses as compressed WARC in object storage partitioned by date and host, with metadata in a columnar table, so any parse can be replayed later
Handle failure: kill 30 percent of workers during a test crawl and show no URL is lost or double-counted beyond the idempotency guarantee

Expose metrics: pages per second, success rate, p95 fetch latency, queue age per host, and a dashboard; sustain 20 pages per second average (about 50M per month) with a 5 worker fleet or state the scaling factor
Write a runbook for blocks: how to detect, back off, and escalate to the site owner

examples.title: Per-host politeness scheduler
examples.code:
def next_ready(hosts, now):
    # hosts: heap of (next_allowed_ts, host)
    ts, host = hosts[0]
    if ts > now:
        return None
    heapq.heappop(hosts)
    url = frontier[host].pop_best()
    heapq.heappush(hosts, (now + delay[host], host))
    return url
examples.output: Returns a URL only when its host is allowed again; with delay 1.0 two fetches for the same host are always at least 1 second apart

examples.title: Crawl health snapshot
examples.code:
fetch_rate=21.4/s  ok=96.8%  429=0.6%  5xx=1.9%
frontier=38.2M urls  oldest_ready_age=14m
dup_url_rate=61%  dup_content_rate=9%
examples.output: Shape of the dashboard; values vary

notes: Spider traps (calendars, session ids, infinite faceted search) will eat your budget; cap depth, per-host page count and URL length.
Politeness is also pragmatic: gentle crawlers get fewer blocks and survive longer.
Store raw bytes first; parsers change monthly, re-fetching 50M pages is expensive.

title: Self-Healing Rate Extraction
description: Detect site layout changes and recover automatically so loan rate data stays accurate for borrowers.
overview: Detect site layout changes and recover automatically so loan rate data stays accurate for borrowers.
tasks: Define a data contract per source (JSON Schema: required fields, types, ranges such as price greater than 0 and under 100000, currency in a known set)
Layer extractors by robustness: embedded JSON-LD or API endpoints first, then semantic CSS selectors, then XPath, then an LLM or ML fallback on the cleaned DOM; record which layer produced each field
Compute per-run quality metrics per source: field completeness, null rate, distinct-value ratio, and distribution drift (population stability index or KS test against the last 7 days)
Alert when completeness falls below 98 percent or drift PSI exceeds 0.2, with a sample of failing HTML attached; mean time to detect under 15 minutes
Snapshot HTML for a sampled 1 percent of pages and keep a regression corpus of 50 pages per source; run extractors against it in CI

Implement automatic selector repair: when the primary selector returns null, propose candidates by matching previously extracted values in the new DOM, validate against the contract, and open a pull request rather than silently deploying
Quarantine bad records in a dead-letter table and never overwrite last-known-good data with nulls
Report outcomes over 30 days: breakages detected, percent auto-repaired, mean time to repair, and completeness per source in a table

examples.title: Data contract
examples.code:
{"$id":"product.v3","type":"object","required":["sku","price","currency"],
 "properties":{"sku":{"type":"string","minLength":3},
  "price":{"type":"number","exclusiveMinimum":0,"maximum":100000},
  "currency":{"enum":["USD","EUR","GBP"]}}}
examples.output: Records that fail validation go to dead_letter with the failing path, source and HTML snapshot id

examples.title: Quality alert
examples.code:
[ALERT] source=shopA field=price completeness=61% (7d avg 99.2%)
layer_used: css 39%, jsonld 0%, fallback 61%
likely cause: selector .price-now missing; candidate: span[data-test=price]
examples.output: Alert contains cause hypothesis and a link to the auto-generated fix PR

notes: A scraper that returns 200 with an empty list is the worst failure; assert minimum expected record counts per run.
LLM fallbacks are for repair and low volume; cost and nondeterminism make them wrong as the primary path at scale.
Never let a bad run delete good history; write versions, not overwrites.

title: Legal Scraping Governance
description: Make a financial data scraper respect law, terms and ethics, so public data helps people without harming sites.
overview: Make a financial data scraper respect law, terms and ethics, so public data helps people without harming sites.
tasks: Write a source-onboarding checklist covering terms of service review, robots.txt, personal data presence, copyright and database rights, jurisdiction (GDPR, CCPA, CFAA case law such as hiQ v LinkedIn), and an approval record signed by legal
Classify each of your 100 sources into green (public, permitted), amber (terms restrict, seek licence) and red (do not scrape) and produce the register with owner and review date

Implement a PII scanner on ingestion (regex plus NER) that drops or hashes emails, phone numbers and names for sources not approved for personal data, with measured recall above 95 percent on a labelled sample

Reduce block rate without evasion: conditional requests, caching, request spreading, realistic HTTP/2 client behaviour and honest identification; measure block rate before and after (target under 1 percent of requests)
Evaluate alternatives per amber source: official API, data licence, or partner feed, with cost per million records compared to scraping including engineering time
Build an immutable audit log of what was fetched, when, from which source, under which approval, and a data-deletion process that satisfies a takedown request within 72 hours
Respond to takedown: implement a documented process, a kill switch per source within 15 minutes, and test it in a drill
Present a risk report to leadership with the cost of compliance, legal exposure and recommended source portfolio

examples.title: Source register row
examples.code:
source: shopA.example
status: amber
robots_allowed: true
tos_clause: "3.2 prohibits automated access"
pii: false
decision: seek_license
reviewed_by: legal@acme.com
review_due: 2027-02-01
examples.output: Pipeline refuses to schedule any source whose status is red or whose review_due date has passed

examples.title: Kill switch
examples.code: $ crawlctl source disable shopA.example --reason "takedown #4412" --purge-after 72h
examples.output: shopA.example disabled; 0 in-flight fetches; purge scheduled 2026-11-10T12:00Z; audit entry 88321 written

notes: Circumventing authentication or technical access controls moves you from a grey area to a serious legal one; never do it.
Ask for the data first; many sites sell or give a feed, and the relationship is worth more than the scrape.
Law differs by country and changes; treat this as engineering input to legal advice, not a substitute for it.

title: Causal Study of a Bank Fee Change
description: Measure whether a fee change really affected customers' choices, so regulators and banks see the real impact.
overview: Measure whether a fee change really affected customers' choices, so regulators and banks see the real impact.
tasks: Write a pre-registered analysis plan: hypothesis, primary metric (7-day revenue per new user), guardrail metrics, population, and stopping rule, committed before looking at outcome data
Run a power calculation for an A/B test: baseline mean and variance from 90 days of history, minimum detectable effect of 3 percent, alpha 0.05, power 0.8, giving a required sample size per arm
Check randomisation with a sample ratio mismatch chi-square test (flag p below 0.001) and covariate balance with standardised mean differences under 0.1
Apply variance reduction with CUPED using pre-experiment spend and report the reduction in confidence-interval width
Estimate the effect with a bootstrap or Welch test, report the point estimate, 95 percent interval and p-value, and correct for multiple metrics with Benjamini-Hochberg
For the launch already shipped to everyone, estimate impact with difference-in-differences and a synthetic control, test parallel trends with placebo dates, and compare estimates to the A/B result
Segment effects (new vs returning, country) with caution, using pre-specified segments and interaction tests to avoid forking paths
Deliver a two-page decision memo: effect with interval in dollars, risks, recommendation, and what would change your mind; present it to a non-technical audience
Store code, data snapshot and results in a reproducible repository with a locked environment

examples.title: Power calculation
examples.code:
from statsmodels.stats.power import TTestIndPower
sd, base = 42.0, 31.0
d = (0.03 * base) / sd
n = TTestIndPower().solve_power(effect_size=d, alpha=0.05, power=0.8)
print(round(n))
examples.output: about 32000 users per arm (shape: the number scales with 1 over d squared; your values depend on your variance)

examples.title: Result summary
examples.code:
Revenue per new user, 7d
control 31.02  treatment 32.10
lift +3.5%  95% CI [+0.8%, +6.2%]  p=0.011 (CUPED)
SRM p=0.62  guardrail churn: no significant change
examples.output: Interval, not just the point estimate, goes in the memo; the 12 percent claim from before/after is not supported

notes: Peeking at an A/B test daily and stopping at significance inflates false positives badly; use a fixed horizon or sequential methods.
Before/after comparisons are confounded by seasonality, marketing and mix; always find a control.
A null result with a tight interval is a valuable finding; say so.

title: Metric Framework for Payments Impact
description: Reconcile conflicting payment metrics across teams so a decision about customer fees rests on one truth.
overview: Reconcile conflicting payment metrics across teams so a decision about customer fees rests on one truth.
tasks: Interview stakeholders and document 10 core metrics (for example monthly active customers, net revenue retention, CAC payback) with precise definitions covering grain, time zone, filters and exclusions
Build a metric tree linking the north-star metric to 3 levels of input metrics, and show which are leading vs lagging

Implement definitions once in a semantic layer (dbt metrics, Cube or LookML) so every dashboard queries the same logic; add tests such as not_null, unique and a reconciliation test against finance within 0.5 percent
Reconcile the three conflicting active-customer numbers: produce a bridge table explaining every difference in counts (duplicates, trial accounts, timezone, definition) and agree a single definition
Establish metric ownership with a named owner, change log and review cadence; require a pull request and an impact note for any definition change
Perform one deep-dive analysis (for example churn drivers using survival analysis or cohort retention) that yields a recommendation, with sensitivity checks and stated limitations
Track the decision: record the action taken, expected impact, and measured result after 90 days, with a counterfactual method such as holdout or difference-in-differences
Report the impact in currency, for example 1.4 million dollars of retained revenue per year with interval, and a retrospective of what you would do differently

examples.title: Metric definition as code
examples.code:
metrics:
  - name: active_customers
    description: Paying accounts with at least one billable event in the month, UTC, excluding internal and trial
    type: count_distinct
    sql: account_id
    filter: "is_internal = false and plan <> 'trial'"
    time_grain: month
    owner: finance-analytics
examples.output: All dashboards read this definition; a CI test compares the monthly value to the finance ledger and fails above 0.5 percent difference

examples.title: Bridge table
examples.code:
Marketing count          48,210
- trial accounts         -3,940
- duplicate emails         -612
+ late-arriving events     +180
= Finance count          43,838
examples.output: Every gap is explained and assigned an owner

notes: Politics beat SQL here; get an executive sponsor to arbitrate definitions before you build.
A metric nobody owns will drift; ownership and a change log matter more than the tool.
Impact claims need a counterfactual, or finance will rightly discount them.

title: Reproducible Financial Reporting
description: Create analysis templates and checks so every published financial number is reproducible for the public.
overview: Create analysis templates and checks so every published financial number is reproducible for the public.
tasks: Define an analysis project template: data/ (immutable raw), src/, notebooks/, reports/, a locked environment (uv or conda-lock), a Makefile or DVC pipeline, and a README with question, method, decision and owner
Make runs reproducible: pin data snapshots with DVC or lakeFS hashes, fix random seeds, and require that make report rebuilds all outputs from raw data on a clean machine in CI within 15 minutes
Strip notebook outputs and enforce formatting with nbstripout, ruff and jupytext pairing; execute notebooks headlessly in CI with papermill to catch hidden state
Write an analysis review checklist covering population definition, join cardinality, survivorship bias, timezone, multiple comparisons, and unit sanity checks; require one reviewer sign-off
Add automated data assertions (Great Expectations or pandera) at pipeline entry: row counts within 5 percent of expected, no duplicate keys, ranges valid; failing checks block publication
Build a published-results registry where every number in a report links to the commit, data hash and query that produced it
Run a replication audit: choose 10 past analyses, attempt to reproduce each, and report the percentage that reproduce exactly, within tolerance, or not at all
Train the team with a 90 minute workshop and track adoption (target 80 percent of new analyses using the template within a quarter) and the drop in post-publication corrections

examples.title: Reproducibility pipeline
examples.code:
stages:
  clean:
    cmd: python src/clean.py data/raw/orders.parquet data/clean/orders.parquet
    deps: [src/clean.py, data/raw/orders.parquet]
    outs: [data/clean/orders.parquet]
  model:
    cmd: python src/model.py
    deps: [data/clean/orders.parquet, src/model.py]
    metrics: [reports/metrics.json]
examples.output:
$ dvc repro
Stage 'clean' didn't change, skipping
Running stage 'model' ... done

examples.title: Replication audit result
examples.code:
Analyses attempted: 10
Exact reproduction: 3
Within tolerance (1%): 4
Failed (missing data or env): 3
examples.output: Baseline before the standard; the target after a quarter is 9 of 10 exact

notes: Hidden notebook state (cells run out of order) is the single biggest source of irreproducible results; execute top to bottom in CI.
Raw data must be immutable; fix problems in code so the fix is visible and repeatable.
Standards stick when the template saves time on day one, not when they add paperwork.

title: Out-of-Core Pipeline for Transaction Data
description: Cut a 6-hour transactions job to under 20 minutes so monthly statements reach customers on time.
overview: Cut a 6-hour transactions job to under 20 minutes so monthly statements reach customers on time.
tasks: Establish a baseline: wall time, peak RSS (memory_profiler or tracemalloc, /usr/bin/time -v) and a result checksum; keep the original output as a golden file
Profile with cProfile and line_profiler or py-spy to locate the top 3 hot spots; record time share for each

Reduce memory using explicit dtypes: category for low-cardinality strings, int32 or float32 where safe, nullable Int64 and string[pyarrow]; show a memory_usage(deep=True) before and after (target at least 70 percent reduction)
Replace row-wise apply and iterrows with vectorised operations, merge and groupby with transform; show a speedup of at least 50x on the hottest function using benchmarks with timeit
Read Parquet with column pruning and predicate pushdown (pyarrow filters) and partition data by date; read only needed columns and row groups

examples.title: Per-pixel min-max downsampling
examples.code:
def minmax_downsample(x, y, width):
    idx = np.linspace(0, len(x), width + 1, dtype=int)
    keep = []
    for a, b in zip(idx[:-1], idx[1:]):
        seg = y[a:b]
        keep += [a + seg.argmin(), a + seg.argmax()]
    keep = sorted(set(keep))
    return x[keep], y[keep]

def test_features_use_only_past(df, cutoff):
    f_full = build_features(df)
    f_cut = build_features(df[df.ts <= cutoff])
    row = f_full[f_full.ts == cutoff].drop(columns='y')

from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL
res = STL(y, period=1440, robust=True).fit().resid
mad = np.median(np.abs(res - np.median(res)))
score = 0.6745 * (res - np.median(res)) / mad
anomalies = np.abs(score) > 4

  link_type='dedupe_only',
  blocking_rules_to_generate_predictions=[block_on('postcode','substr(surname,1,2)'), block_on('email_canon')],
  comparisons=[cl.JaroWinklerAtThresholds('surname',[0.92,0.8]), cl.ExactMatch('dob'), cl.LevenshteinAtThresholds('postcode',1)])
examples.output: Linker trains with EM; predict() yields pairs with match_probability, e.g. 0.998 for same email and similar names

examples.title: Evaluation
examples.code:
threshold  precision  recall   pairs_for_review
0.99       0.998      0.81     0
0.90       0.985      0.92     41,200
0.50       0.91       0.97     212,000
examples.output: Shape; pick auto-merge at the first row and review the middle band

notes: Transitive closure turns two good matches into a bad cluster of strangers; cap cluster size and inspect the largest ones by hand.
Keep an unmerge capability and source lineage; legal and customer complaints will require it.
Test on hard cases: twins, father and son at one address, common names like Wei Zhang.

title: Data Quality SLAs for Banking
description: Monitor data quality across 200 tables so customers' statements are never built on bad data.
overview: Monitor data quality across 200 tables so customers' statements are never built on bad data.
tasks: Rank 200 tables by criticality using lineage and downstream usage; designate the top 30 as tier 1 with owners and SLAs (freshness within 2 hours, completeness above 99.5 percent)

Define check types per table: schema, volume (row count within a seasonal expected band using a rolling median and MAD), freshness, uniqueness, referential integrity, value distributions, and cross-table reconciliation
Implement checks with Great Expectations, Soda or dbt tests, run as part of the pipeline so failures block downstream publication for tier 1 tables (circuit breaker) instead of only alerting
Add anomaly detection on column-level metrics (null fraction, mean, distinct count) with learned seasonality, and tune to under 2 false alerts per week
Establish data contracts between producers and consumers: JSON Schema or protobuf in the producer repository, compatibility checked in CI so a breaking column change fails the producer build
Quarantine failing records to a dead-letter table with the reason code, and build a repair workflow that reprocesses them once fixed
Create an incident process: severity levels, a status page for data, root cause categories, and a blameless post-mortem for every tier 1 incident
Publish a quality scorecard per domain, and measure impact over a quarter: incidents reaching a dashboard down by 70 percent, mean time to detect under 30 minutes, mean time to resolve under 4 hours

examples.title: Volume check with seasonal band
examples.code:
WITH hist AS (
  SELECT percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY n) AS med
  FROM daily_counts
  WHERE dow = extract(dow from current_date) AND day >= current_date - 56)
SELECT n, med, abs(n - med) / med AS dev
FROM today, hist WHERE abs(n - med) / med > 0.25;
examples.output: Returns a row, and the pipeline halts publication, when today's count deviates more than 25 percent from the median for the same weekday

examples.title: Contract check in producer CI
examples.code:
$ datacontract test orders.yaml
schema: removed column 'discount_code' is breaking for consumers [finance_mart, growth_dash]
RESULT: FAILED
examples.output: The producer team sees which consumers would break before merging

notes: Alerts with no owner decay into noise; every check needs a named responder.
Blocking publication is costly when checks are flaky, so prove precision on history before enabling circuit breakers.
Fix at the source; cleaning downstream hides the problem and creates divergent versions of truth.

title: Privacy-Safe Anonymisation of Customer Data
description: Remove personal details from datasets and measure re-identification risk so customers' privacy is protected.
overview: Remove personal details from datasets and measure re-identification risk so customers' privacy is protected.
tasks: Scan 500 datasets for PII using regex validators (Luhn for cards, checksum for national ids), column-name heuristics and an NER model (Presidio), and report findings with confidence; measure recall above 95 percent on a labelled sample of 2,000 columns
Classify columns (direct identifier, quasi-identifier, sensitive, public) in a catalogue and tag them so access policies can follow tags

Apply transformations by class: tokenisation or HMAC pseudonymisation with a managed key for joinable ids, generalisation of dates to month and ages to 5-year bands, truncation of postcodes, and suppression of free text

Measure re-identification risk with k-anonymity (target k at least 10 over the quasi-identifier set), l-diversity for sensitive attributes, and a uniqueness check; document the share of unique records before and after
For aggregate outputs apply differential privacy (for example Laplace noise with epsilon 1.0 and a privacy budget ledger) and show accuracy loss versus raw counts
Measure utility: compare model AUC or aggregate statistics on raw vs anonymised data and keep the loss under 3 percent for the agreed use cases
Implement erasure: a subject-to-token index allowing deletion across the lake, warehouse and backups' retention window within 30 days, with proof via an audit report
Run a red-team re-identification test linking the released data with a public auxiliary dataset and report the success rate (target under 1 percent)
Deliver a data protection impact assessment and a runbook, and obtain sign-off from the privacy officer

examples.title: k-anonymity check
examples.code:
SELECT age_band, zip3, sex, count(*) AS k
FROM released_patients
GROUP BY 1,2,3
HAVING count(*) < 10
ORDER BY k;
examples.output:
age_band | zip3 | sex | k
 85+     | 998  | F   | 2     -- these groups must be generalised further or suppressed
(0 rows is the goal)

examples.title: Deterministic pseudonym
examples.output: The same email always maps to the same token (joins work), and cannot be reversed without the key; rotate keys through the key manager

notes: Plain hashing of low-entropy values such as phone numbers or birth dates is reversible by brute force; use keyed HMAC.
Combinations of harmless columns (zip, birth date, sex) identify most people; test quasi-identifier sets, not columns alone.
Backups and logs are where erased data survives; include them in the design.

title: Profiling Tool for Financial Datasets
description: Profile 1,000 financial datasets for anomalies so regulators spot problems early.
overview: Profile 1,000 financial datasets for anomalies so regulators spot problems early.
tasks: List the checks an expert runs on any dataset (types, nulls, cardinality, duplicates, ranges, skew, outliers, correlations, time coverage, key uniqueness) and prioritise by how often each finds real problems, using 30 past incidents as evidence

Implement profiling with single-pass sketches so a 500 GB table profiles in under 15 minutes: HyperLogLog for distinct counts, t-digest for quantiles, and Count-Min for heavy hitters, with error bounds documented

Detect semantic issues beyond statistics: unit mismatches (for example centimetres vs metres via bimodal distributions), placeholder values (9999, 1970-01-01, N/A), constant columns, and mixed formats using regex families
Compute dataset-to-dataset drift (PSI, KS, Jensen-Shannon) between snapshots and between train and serving data, with thresholds per column type
Score severity (info, warn, critical) and rank findings so a report opens with the 5 most important issues
Generate an HTML report per dataset with distributions, missingness matrix and correlation heatmap that loads in under 3 seconds, plus a machine-readable JSON for CI
Validate the tool: seed 40 synthetic defects into 10 real datasets and measure detection rate (target at least 90 percent) and false-positive findings per dataset (under 3)
Run a study with 8 analysts: time to first insight with and without the tool, and issues found; report the median saving

examples.title: Report excerpt
examples.code:
Dataset: orders_2026_10   rows: 48,201,113   profiled in 6m12s
[CRITICAL] unit_price: 4.1% of values equal 9999 (placeholder?)
[CRITICAL] created_at: 0 rows after 2026-10-19 (stale feed)
[WARN]     country: cardinality 412 vs ISO max 249 (case or typo variants)
[WARN]     amount drift vs 2026-09: PSI 0.31
examples.output: Shape of the output; findings are ranked by severity then by affected rows

examples.title: Streaming sketches
examples.code:
from datasketches import hll_sketch, kll_floats_sketch
h, q = hll_sketch(14), kll_floats_sketch(200)
for v in column_iter:
    h.update(v); q.update(float(v))
print(h.get_estimate(), q.get_quantile(0.99))
examples.output: Estimated distinct count within about 1 percent and p99 within a small rank error, using constant memory

notes: Exact distinct counts and quantiles do not scale; sketches with stated error bounds are the correct trade.
Statistical outliers are often the real data; flag them, do not remove them.
The best finding is the one that changes a pipeline fix, so link every finding to a recommended action.

title: Investigation of a Payment Event Log
description: Investigate a 300-million-row payment log to find why customers' payments failed.
overview: Investigate a 300-million-row payment log to find why customers' payments failed.
tasks: Write the question and success criteria, then sample sensibly (stratified by day and platform) to work interactively while validating that conclusions hold on the full data via DuckDB or Spark
Reverse-engineer the schema: infer event types, session boundaries, funnel stages and identifiers, and document in a data dictionary with confidence level and sources of truth
Establish data trustworthiness first: event counts per day per platform, instrumentation changes (release dates), bot traffic and duplicate event ratios, and timezone effects

Decompose the metric drop with a segment contribution analysis (platform, country, acquisition channel, app version), computing how much each segment explains using Shapley or mix-shift vs rate-shift decomposition
Test hypotheses explicitly: log each (hypothesis, test, result, decision) in a table, including those ruled out, and correct for multiple comparisons when scanning many segments
Check for Simpson's paradox and survivorship bias by comparing aggregate and stratified rates
Dig into the top finding with funnels, cohort and survival curves, and examine raw sessions manually (read 30 sessions) to confirm the mechanism
Report: ranked causes with estimated share of the 8 percent drop, confidence, recommended actions and a monitoring metric, plus what you could not determine

examples.title: Mix-shift vs rate-shift decomposition
examples.code:
m = df.groupby('segment').agg(w0=('w0','sum'), w1=('w1','sum'), r0=('r0','mean'), r1=('r1','mean'))
m['mix']  = (m.w1 - m.w0) * (m.r0 - m.r0.mean())
m['rate'] = m.w1 * (m.r1 - m.r0)
print(m[['mix','rate']].sum())
examples.output:
mix    -0.011
rate   -0.069   -> most of the drop is within-segment conversion, not audience mix (shape; values vary)

examples.title: Hypothesis log
examples.code:
H1 bot spike inflates sessions       ruled out (bot share 1.1% -> 1.2%)
H2 app v5.2 broke checkout on Android supported (Android v5.2 conv -31%)
H3 paid channel mix shifted           minor (explains 0.9 of 8 points)
examples.output: Each hypothesis has a test and a decision, so reviewers can follow the reasoning

notes: Check the instrumentation before the product; a logging change causes more fake drops than customers do.
Scanning 200 segments will produce spurious wins; pre-limit dimensions or correct for multiplicity.
Reading raw sessions is slow and indispensable; patterns appear that no aggregate shows.

title: Statistical Reasoning Programme for Analysts
description: Teach analysts to reason about data so public financial reports are sound.
overview: Teach analysts to reason about data so public financial reports are sound.
tasks: Run a needs assessment: review 20 recent analyses, classify the errors (selection bias, confounding, misread distributions, p-hacking), and base the syllabus on the top 8

Design 6 weekly modules of 90 minutes: distributions and summaries, missingness, bias and sampling, correlation vs causation, uncertainty and intervals, and communicating findings, each with a learning objective stated as an observable skill
Build hands-on notebooks with seeded real-style datasets containing planted traps (Simpson's paradox, survivorship, duplicates, unit errors, leaked target) and a facilitator key listing each trap
Create a pre-test and post-test of 20 scenario questions with validated difficulty; target an average gain of at least 25 percentage points
Introduce a peer review rubric with 10 criteria and run review sessions where each analyst critiques another's analysis using it
Deliver a capstone where each participant explores an unseen dataset in 3 hours and submits a report graded blind on traps found (out of 8), correctness of claims and clarity
Collect feedback each week and iterate the next session; record attendance and completion above 85 percent
Evaluate impact after 90 days: reviewer-found defects per analysis, comparing participants to a control group of non-participants, and share open materials on the internal wiki for reuse

examples.title: Planted trap with facilitator key
examples.code:
# Exercise 3: hospital recovery data
# Surface result: treatment A recovery 78 percent vs treatment B 83 percent
# Planted trap: B was mostly given to mild cases (Simpson's paradox)
df.groupby(['severity','treatment']).recovered.mean().unstack()
examples.output:
treatment        A     B
severity
mild          0.93  0.87
severe        0.73  0.69
# A wins in both strata although B wins overall

examples.title: Assessment result
examples.code:
cohort   n    pre   post   gain   capstone traps found (of 8)
program  40   54%   81%    +27    5.9
control  25   55%   58%    +3     2.8
examples.output: Shape; values vary

notes: People learn pitfalls from being fooled by a safe example, so let them reach the wrong answer before you explain.
Use data from your own business; abstract datasets do not transfer.
Measure on behaviour change in real work, not on workshop satisfaction.

title: Frontend Architecture for Banking Teams
description: Let 12 banking teams ship independently so customers get fixes without waiting for other teams.
overview: Let 12 banking teams ship independently so customers get fixes without waiting for other teams.
tasks: Measure the baseline: CI duration, deploy frequency, lead time, change failure rate (DORA), build time, bundle size and the cross-team dependency graph generated with madge or Nx graph

Write an ADR comparing a modular monolith with enforced boundaries, Module Federation micro-frontends, and an iframe or edge-composed approach; record the decision with trade-offs and the team-topology reasoning
Define domain boundaries aligned to teams, expose each module only through a public API, and enforce with ESLint boundaries or Nx module-boundary rules so cross-module deep imports fail CI
Adopt a monorepo with Nx or Turborepo with remote caching and affected-only builds; target CI under 10 minutes for a typical change and cache hit rate above 80 percent

Create shared foundations: design tokens (Style Dictionary), a component library with Storybook and visual tests, a typed API client generated from OpenAPI, and a shared auth/session module, versioned with semantic versioning
Implement independent deployment: each team can deploy its module without coordinating, behind feature flags with progressive rollout and automatic rollback on error-rate increase
Use the strangler pattern to migrate the five busiest areas one at a time while the app stays shippable, tracking the percent migrated
Keep runtime cost under control: shared dependencies deduplicated (single React instance), total JS per route under budget, and Core Web Vitals not regressing
Report results after two quarters: deploys per team per week, lead time reduction, and incident count; collect developer-experience survey scores

examples.title: Boundary rule
examples.output: error: A project tagged scope:checkout cannot depend on libs tagged scope:search

examples.title: Delivery metrics
examples.code:
metric               before    after (2 quarters)
CI p50               55 min    9 min
deploys / week       1         34 (team-independent)
change failure rate  22%       9%
examples.output: Shape; values vary
